implementation_notes: Every Ruby object already knows how to clone itself: dup returns a shallow, unfrozen copy, clone also copies the frozen and singleton-class state, and both run initialize_copy (through initialize_dup/initialize_clone), which is where a class deep-copies its own mutable state or resets identity. The GoF step of declaring a cloning interface disappears because the mechanism lives on Object; what remains is the per-class decision of what to duplicate, which is exactly the method the pattern leaves to the ConcretePrototype. ActiveRecord builds its dup on this to copy a record without its id.
code_sketch:
class Campaign
  attr_accessor :code, :limits

  def initialize_copy(other)   # runs for both dup and clone
    super
    @limits = other.limits.dup  # deep-copy the mutable part
  end
end

template = Campaign.new
template.code = "BF24"
mine = template.dup            # copy, then specialise
pitfalls: dup/clone are shallow: instance variables pointing at mutable objects (arrays, hashes, nested objects) are shared - deep-copy them in initialize_copy or use Marshal round-trip for graphs.
clone keeps frozen and singleton state (clone(freeze: false) opts out) while dup drops extended modules; the difference is a deliberate choice, not an accident.
initialize_copy must call super or the inherited copy behaviour is skipped; and allocate-based copying never runs initialize, so invariants established there are not re-applied.
